title: Indienne Brings Chicago's Only Michelin-Starred Indian Cuisine to New York's Hudson Yards
excerpt: Chef Sujan Sarkar opens a 34-seat outpost of his acclaimed progressive Indian tasting menu restaurant, joining a surge of high-profile Indian fine dining in Manhattan.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Chef Sujan Sarkar opens Indienne New York, a 34-seat Michelin-starred restaurant from Chicago.
  • The restaurant features three nine-course tasting menus priced at $195 and $175.
  • Indienne joins a growing trend of high-end Indian dining in Manhattan.
  • Sarkar is also launching two more concepts: British-Indian chophouse Elder and cocktail bar Apas.
  • The expansion signifies a cultural milestone for Indian cuisine in the U.S. fine dining scene.
  • Chef Sujan Sarkar has opened Indienne New York in Hudson Yards, an evolution of his Michelin-starred Chicago flagship that earned its star within its first year in 2023
  • The 34-seat restaurant offers three nine-course tasting menus — non-vegetarian at $195, vegetarian and vegan at $175 — featuring progressive Indian cuisine blending regional flavors with European techniques
  • Indienne joins a wave of ambitious Indian restaurant openings in New York, including Houston's Musaafer and London's Ambassadors Clubhouse
  • Sarkar, a 2024 James Beard finalist originally from Kolkata, is also opening two more concepts in the same building: British-Indian chophouse Elder and cocktail bar Apas

Chef Sujan Sarkar has brought his Michelin-starred Indienne from Chicago to New York, opening a 34-seat progressive Indian restaurant inside Henry Hall, a luxury residential building in Hudson Yards. The restaurant opened on May 28, marking a homecoming for the Kolkata-born chef who first made his name in New York with the modern Indian gastrobar Baar Baar in the East Village in 2017.

Indienne earned a Michelin star within its first year of opening in Chicago's River North neighborhood in 2022 — the first and still only starred Indian restaurant in the city. It also landed on "Best New Restaurant" lists from Esquire and Bon Appétit, and Sarkar was named a 2024 James Beard Award finalist.

Progressive Indian Cuisine at the Highest Level

The New York outpost centers on three distinct nine-course tasting menus: non-vegetarian priced at $195, and vegetarian and vegan options at $175. The progression begins with playful, chaat-inspired dishes before moving into seasonal courses that showcase layered spices, varied textures and regional Indian influences refined through classical European techniques.

"I want to be a true representation of Indian food in America, which can be on par with the top restaurants in the city and the country — and in the world."

— Sujan Sarkar, Chef-Owner of Indienne

Beverage Director Chris Farrell has built a wine program focused on small-production, terroir-driven bottles. The restaurant also features a sustainability-focused cocktail menu using ingredients recycled from the kitchen, alongside a customizable Gin & Tonic program.

A Wave of Indian Fine Dining in New York

Indienne arrives alongside a historic surge of ambitious Indian restaurants in Manhattan. Houston's Musaafer and London's Ambassadors Clubhouse have recently opened outposts, joining an already strong roster that includes Vikas Khanna's Bungalow and Semma, which holds the distinction of being the first Indian restaurant in New York to earn a Michelin star.

The trend signals a broader shift in how Indian cuisine is positioned in the American fine dining conversation — no longer relegated to casual or mid-range dining, but competing directly at the highest tier.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, the expansion of Michelin-level Indian dining in the United States's most competitive restaurant market represents a cultural milestone. Sarkar, who spent 12 years in modern European and French kitchens before pivoting to Indian cuisine, sees his work as proof that the depth and complexity of Indian food deserves its place alongside any global cuisine.

The interiors, designed by MAPA Mueller, feature textured finishes, sculptural lighting and Holi-inspired paintings by Chicago artist Ken Andjulis. Two additional concepts from Sarkar — British-Indian chophouse Elder and cocktail bar Apas — will open in the same building later this year.

Looking Ahead

Sarkar plans to split his time between Chicago and New York, calling it "a very easy commute." He does 650 to 670 covers a week at the Chicago original and has expanded his Windy City footprint with three additional restaurants: Sifr, Nadu, and South Asian bakery Swadesi. But the original Indienne, he says, will always be home.
